canonicalExplanation.summary: The `<title>` names the page in browser tabs, bookmarks, history, screen-reader announcements and search results — so each page needs a **unique, specific** title, most specific part first: "Variables in C – Codestead". The `<meta name="description">` is a short summary that search engines **may** show under the link. Neither replaces the visible `<h1>`, and no tag can guarantee a ranking.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You have ten Codestead tabs open, and every one says "Home". Which is the C variables lesson? A screen-reader user switching windows hears "Home" ten times too. The lesson page title reads Variables in C - Codestead rather than the same Home title used everywhere. In this lesson you'll author metadata for a small multi-page site without promising ranking behavior.

```predict
{"question": "Can a meta description replace the page's h1?", "options": ["Yes, it's the page summary", "No — it's not shown on the page; the visible h1 is still needed"], "answer": 1, "why": "The description lives in the head and is only (sometimes) used by search results. The h1 is the page's visible main heading."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Document foundations**, **Text and page semantics** and **Forms and native controls** modules, plus the **Standards-mode document skeleton** and **Relative and absolute URLs**.

sections.heading: The model: title names the page, description summarises it
sections.body:
```html
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Variables in C – Codestead</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Learn how C variables store values, how to declare and initialise them, and common beginner mistakes.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://codestead.example/c/variables/">
</head>
```

| Tag | Used by | Tip |
|---|---|---|
| `title`. | tabs, bookmarks, screen readers, search results. | unique; specific part first. |
| `meta description`. | possibly search snippets. | 1–2 honest sentences. |
| `link rel=canonical`. | search engines. | the preferred URL for duplicate pages. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Will a perfect description guarantee first place in search results?", "answer": "No. Search engines decide ranking and may even rewrite snippets. Good metadata makes pages clearer — it doesn't promise rankings."}
```

sections.heading: Specific first

includes: Write unique, specific titles and honest meta descriptions for each page.
Explain what title, description and canonical are used for — without promising rankings.
excludes: Open Graph and social sharing tags.

outcomes: Author metadata for a small multi-page site without promising ranking behavior.

examples.title: Unique titles for every lesson
examples.situation: The lesson page title reads Variables in C - Codestead rather than the same Home title used everywhere.
walkthrough: **Before:** every page's title read "Home", so tabs and history were indistinguishable.
**After:** the lesson page title reads "Variables in C – Codestead"; the arrays lesson reads "Arrays in C – Codestead".
**Check:** open several tabs and the browser will render each unique title; a screen reader announces it when the page loads.
examples.result: Every page can be told apart in tabs, bookmarks, history and search results.

examples.title: The keyword-stuffed description
examples.situation: A page's description reads "C, C programming, learn C, best C course, free C, C tutorial, C variables…".
walkthrough: It doesn't describe the page to a human.
Search engines often ignore or rewrite such text.
Fix: "Learn how C variables store values, how to declare and initialise them, and common beginner mistakes."
examples.result: The description now honestly summarises the page for people scanning results.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The meta description is the page's accessible heading and replaces an h1.
misconceptions.correction: The description is head metadata that search engines may use for snippets; it isn't displayed or announced as a heading. The page still needs a unique title and a visible h1.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why can't the description replace the h1?

analogy.example: A title is like the **spine label on a book** — you find the book on the shelf by it. The description is the **blurb on the back cover** — helpful, but the shop decides where the book goes on the shelf (ranking).
limitations: Books have one spine label; web pages need one per page.
Shops (search engines) may rewrite the blurb.

remediation.explanation: For each page ask: **If ten tabs were open, would this title stand out? Does the description honestly say what's on the page?**

recap.summary: To author metadata for a small multi-page site, give each page a unique title with the specific part first, an honest meta description, and a canonical URL where needed. The h1 is still required, and metadata never guarantees ranking behavior.
